title: The Weekend Client Database Emergency
context: It is Friday at 6:30 PM. A critical client deadline is scheduled for Monday morning, and you plan to work from home on your personal desktop computer. You are tempted to upload the 50,000-record client database to your personal Google Drive or email it to your personal Gmail account.
dilemma: How do you handle the client data so you can finish the analysis over the weekend?

choices.text: Upload the CSV to personal Google Drive so you can easily access it on your home PC.
choices.feedback: Violates Sec 4.5 (Cloud Storage) & Sec 8.2. Personal Google Drive lacks corporate DLP, access governance, and NDA compliance.

choices.text: Email the spreadsheet to your personal Gmail account with 'Urgent' in the subject line.
choices.feedback: Severe violation of Sec 4.1 & Sec 4.5. Personal webmail is monitored for data exfiltration and breaches data residency laws.

choices.text: Use your corporate-issued laptop connected to the corporate VPN, keeping all data inside approved cloud tenants.
choices.feedback: Correct decision! Keeping data inside the managed perimeter ensures encryption, audit logging, and zero unauthorized exposure.

title: Summarizing Proprietary Source Code with AI
context: You are debugging a complex internal authentication module. An online public AI coding tool claims to diagnose performance bottlenecks in seconds if you paste the entire codebase and SQL schema into its prompt window.
dilemma: Should you paste the source code into the free online AI assistant?

choices.text: Paste the code into the public AI tool, because it's only code logic and not customer names.
choices.feedback: Violates Sec 9.1 (Generative AI) & Sec 11.1 (Source Code). Public AI services may train on prompt inputs and store internal architecture permanently.

choices.text: Remove database passwords from the code, then paste the remaining 5,000 lines of proprietary code into the public AI tool.
choices.feedback: Still a violation. Proprietary intellectual property, business logic, and schema structures remain exposed to third-party retention.

choices.text: Use only company-approved enterprise AI tools with signed zero-data-retention agreements, or consult a senior internal engineer.
choices.feedback: Excellent decision! Enterprise-contracted AI protects corporate IP while preserving developer productivity.

title: The Impersonated CEO's Boardroom Emergency
context: You receive an email from 'Sarah Jenkins <sjenkins.ceo.board@gmail.com>' with display name 'Sarah Jenkins (CEO)'. The email states: 'I am trapped in an offsite investor meeting with bad reception. I need you to purchase 10 Apple gift cards ($100 each) for client gifts immediately and text me the codes. Do not call my office line as my phone is muted.'
dilemma: How do you respond to the CEO's urgent request?

choices.text: Rush to the nearest convenience store, purchase the cards with your personal credit card, and text the photos.
choices.feedback: Classic Business Email Compromise (BEC) scam. Executives never order gift card purchases through personal Gmail accounts.

choices.text: Reply to the Gmail address asking if she can approve an expense reimbursement form first.
choices.feedback: Replying confirms to the attacker that your email address is active and responsive.

choices.text: Do not purchase gift cards. Report the email immediately as executive impersonation via NETRAK.
choices.feedback: Correct! Immediate reporting allows the SOC to block the attacker's domain across the entire enterprise.

title: Airport Wi-Fi and the Urgent Contract
context: While waiting for a flight at an international airport, you connect your company laptop to 'Airport_Public_Free_WiFi'. A client emails you demanding immediate signature on a multi-million-dollar contract.
dilemma: How should you access corporate systems to sign and transmit the contract?

choices.text: Open Chrome in Incognito mode and access the contract portal directly.
choices.feedback: Incognito mode provides zero transport encryption. Attackers running rogue access points can intercept session cookies.

choices.text: Connect to the corporate VPN client first, verify the secure tunnel, then review and sign the contract.
choices.feedback: Safe and compliant! Corporate VPN encrypts all traffic from the endpoint, shielding payloads from open Wi-Fi sniffing.

choices.text: Ask another passenger to share their personal Wi-Fi password instead.
choices.feedback: Third-party guest hotspots are still untrusted networks.

title: The Suspicious Link and Password Prompt
context: You received an email that looked like a shipping notification from FedEx. You clicked the tracking link, and it redirected to a page that looked like the corporate Microsoft 365 sign-in page. You entered your corporate email and password. Immediately after clicking Submit, the page redirected to a 404 error.
dilemma: What do you do right now?

choices.text: Close the tab, assume it was just a glitch, and continue working on your afternoon tasks.
choices.feedback: Dangerous mistake! You just handed your corporate credentials to a phishing adversary. Immediate action is vital.

choices.text: Immediately disconnect from network/Wi-Fi, report the incident via NETRAK or the SOC hotline, and initiate a password reset.
choices.feedback: Exact right response! Halts active beaconing, notifies security for session revocation, and neutralizes credential abuse.

choices.text: Wait until tomorrow to see if IT calls you about unusual activity.
choices.feedback: Attacker dwell time averages under an hour for credential compromise. Waiting amplifies breach scope.

title: The Labeled Flash Drive in the Parking Lot
context: Walking into the office from the parking lot, you notice a brand new 128GB flash drive with a handwritten label: 'Q4 Executive Compensation & Staffing'.
dilemma: What is the safest action?

choices.text: Plug it into your computer to see whose name is on the document and return it to them.
choices.feedback: Classic USB drop attack! Attackers bait curiosity to deploy keystroke injection or malware directly onto corporate endpoints.

choices.text: Deliver the flash drive directly to the Physical Security or IT Desk without plugging it in.
choices.feedback: Perfect! Security personnel can examine it inside isolated sandbox environments without risking corporate endpoints.

choices.text: Plug it into a colleague's laptop instead to test it.
choices.feedback: Exposes colleague's system to endpoint compromise.

title: Tailgating Through the Secure Lab Door
context: You badge into the secure server and R&D laboratory. A smartly dressed individual carrying two heavy catering boxes approaches quickly behind you and says, 'Could you hold the door? My hands are full!'
dilemma: How do you handle this situation?

choices.text: Hold the door open to be courteous since they have heavy boxes.
choices.feedback: Tailgating (piggybacking) is a primary physical social engineering tactic. Politeness cannot override physical access control.

choices.text: Let the door click shut, and politely explain that security policy requires all entrants to badge in, or escort them to reception.
choices.feedback: Proper protocol. Protects physical boundaries while maintaining a professional, calm demeanor.

choices.text: Swipe your badge twice so they have a badge record under your name.
choices.feedback: You become legally and forensically liable for all unauthorized actions taken by the untracked individual.

title: The Accidental GitHub Commit
context: While pushing code to an internal service, you accidentally commit a `.env` file containing the production Stripe API key to your public personal GitHub account instead of the private enterprise repository.
dilemma: How do you resolve this immediate exposure?

choices.text: Make the public repo private and push a commit removing the file.
choices.feedback: Public Git scraping bots clone repositories within 3 seconds of a commit. The key is already compromised in third-party bot caches.

choices.text: Immediately log into Stripe, revoke/rotate the compromised key, and report the exposure via NETRAK.
choices.feedback: Key invalidation neutralizes the exploit vector immediately, and NETRAK reporting enables incident auditing of API calls.

choices.text: Delete the entire repository on GitHub and don't tell anyone.
choices.feedback: The secret was scraped instantly; hiding the mistake prevents the company from securing the compromised financial channel.

title: Working in a Crowded Coffee Shop
context: You are sitting at an open cafe table preparing a confidential quarterly revenue forecast. A stranger sits at the table directly behind you with their laptop angled toward your screen, while someone else on your left is glancing over frequently.
dilemma: What precautions should you take?

choices.text: Dim your screen brightness slightly and continue reviewing the financial figures.
choices.feedback: Dimming is insufficient to prevent visual eavesdropping on sensitive financial numbers.

choices.text: Attach a physical privacy filter to your screen, position yourself with your back to a solid wall, and avoid viewing confidential figures in plain sight.
choices.feedback: Applying privacy filters and physical spatial awareness stops shoulder surfing in public settings.

choices.text: Take a photo of the numbers on your phone so you can read them quickly instead.
choices.feedback: Photographing confidential data on mobile devices violates data protection and privacy rules.

title: The 3 AM Authenticator Storm
context: Your phone buzzes repeatedly in the middle of the night with 8 consecutive Duo push notifications asking 'Are you logging into Enterprise Okta?'.
dilemma: How do you handle this push fatigue attack?

choices.text: Tap Approve on one prompt so the phone stops buzzing and you can sleep.
choices.feedback: Critical compromise! Approving grants the attacker active access to your enterprise session.

choices.text: Tap 'Deny & Report Fraud' on the prompt, then open NETRAK to notify the SOC and initiate a password reset in the morning.
choices.feedback: Perfect! Denying shuts out the attacker and alerts the monitoring system to freeze the compromised account.

choices.text: Uninstall the Duo app from your phone.
choices.feedback: Fails to alert security while leaving your underlying account credentials compromised.

title: The Fake Internal Audit Call
context: A caller with an authoritative British accent phones your desk: 'Hello, this is Marcus Vance from Corporate Internal Compliance. We are auditing executive directory access. I need you to confirm the personal mobile number and home address of Vice President Davis.'
dilemma: How do you respond to the authoritative caller?

choices.text: Read the VP's personal details because the caller cited internal audit authority.
choices.feedback: Vishing attack! Attackers routinely cite audit or executive teams to intimidate employees into bypassing privacy rules.

choices.text: Refuse to disclose personal employee data over the phone. Request their employee ID, hang up, and verify the inquiry through official channels.
choices.feedback: Standard out-of-band verification procedure. Defeats social engineering pretexts.

choices.text: Offer to email the VP's full personnel file to the caller's personal Gmail.
choices.feedback: Severe violation of PII protection standards.

title: The 'Free' Productivity Browser Extension
context: A popular productivity Chrome extension offers 'One-Click AI Meeting Summaries'. Upon installation, the Chrome Web Store warns: 'This extension requires permission to read and change all your data on all websites you visit.'
dilemma: Should you grant these extensive permissions on your work browser?

choices.text: Click 'Allow' because many popular extensions ask for that permission.
choices.feedback: Extreme risk! An extension with broad DOM access can harvest session cookies, passwords, and confidential customer records.

choices.text: Cancel the installation. Submit a software evaluation request through the IT Corporate Software Portal for an approved alternative.
choices.feedback: Correct protocol. Only IT-vetted extensions may operate within corporate browser environments.

choices.text: Install it in an Incognito window thinking that isolates it.
choices.feedback: Extensions enabled in Incognito still retain full access to active DOM data.

title: Client Requesting WhatsApp Group for Contracts
context: A major enterprise customer says: 'Our executive team only communicates via WhatsApp. Please send the final unredacted pricing sheet and legal terms in our WhatsApp group chat.'
dilemma: How do you navigate this communication request?

choices.text: Upload the pricing sheet to WhatsApp because customer convenience comes first.
choices.feedback: Violates Sec 4.4. Consumer messaging apps bypass corporate records retention, legal discovery, and data governance.

choices.text: Explain that corporate security and compliance policy requires contracts to be shared via authenticated enterprise channels (e.g. encrypted corporate email or customer portal).
choices.feedback: Professional and compliant. Protects commercial agreements within legally auditable repositories.

choices.text: Screenshot each page of the contract and send the pictures on WhatsApp.
choices.feedback: Still transmits confidential enterprise assets through unapproved consumer channels.

title: The Breakroom Parking Validation QR Code
context: A printed flyer taped next to the office water cooler says: 'Building Management: Scan this QR code to claim your free monthly parking validation pass.' Scanning it on your phone opens a webpage asking for your corporate Microsoft credentials.
dilemma: Should you enter your credentials on the mobile page?

choices.text: Enter your corporate credentials so you get free parking validation.
choices.feedback: Quishing attack! Malicious QR codes redirect users to credential harvesting sites on unmanaged mobile phones.

choices.text: Close the page, do not enter any credentials, take a photo of the flyer, and report the physical quishing attempt to Security.
choices.feedback: Outstanding vigilance! Reporting physical social engineering protects all building occupants.

choices.text: Enter fake credentials with vulgar words to test the site.
choices.feedback: Unprofessional and alerts the attacker without assisting formal containment.

title: The Stolen Taxi Laptop
context: While traveling on business, you accidentally leave your corporate laptop in the trunk of a taxi. You have the taxi receipt but the dispatch company cannot reach the driver for at least 3 hours.
dilemma: When should you report the lost device to corporate security?

choices.text: Wait until tomorrow morning in case the driver returns it to your hotel.
choices.feedback: Violates Sec 1.2 (Mandatory 60-minute reporting). Waiting leaves the corporate identity active and increases data theft risk.

choices.text: Report the lost laptop immediately to the Security Operations Center via NETRAK or the 24/7 hotline so remote lock and session revocation can be dispatched.
choices.feedback: Crucial quick reporting! SOC can remotely lock BitLocker keys and invalidate active SSO tokens.

choices.text: Buy a replacement laptop at a local store and set it up yourself so no one notices.
choices.feedback: Severe violation of device governance and unacceptable concealment of an active incident.

title: Open-Sourcing an Internal Utility Library
context: You wrote a helpful React helper component during work hours. You want to publish it to your personal public GitHub account to boost your resume.
dilemma: Can you publish the company-developed code to your personal public repo?

choices.text: Yes, as long as you remove company logos from the CSS.
choices.feedback: Code written on corporate time and systems belongs to the enterprise. Publishing without Open Source Review Board approval violates Sec 11.1.

choices.text: Submit the request through the formal corporate Open Source Review Board for legal and intellectual property clearance.
choices.feedback: Compliant process. Ensures no trade secrets, patent conflicts, or proprietary dependencies are inadvertently released.

choices.text: Publish it anonymously under a pseudonym.
choices.feedback: Still an unauthorized release of proprietary corporate property.

title: Old Printed Customer Contracts in the Bin
context: You are cleaning your desk drawers and find three printed contracts containing customer names, addresses, and credit limits from 2024.
dilemma: How should you dispose of these obsolete physical documents?

choices.text: Throw them in the general blue recycling bin beside your desk.
choices.feedback: Violates Sec 10.2. General recycling bins are not locked and expose customer PII to unauthorized custodial staff or visitors.

choices.text: Deposit the documents into the locked, cross-cut shredding console for certified secure disposal.
choices.feedback: Correct! Locked consoles ensure document chain of custody until industrial destruction.

choices.text: Tear them in half by hand and place them in the kitchen trash.
choices.feedback: Torn documents are easily reconstructed.

title: Public USB Charging Kiosk at the Airport Gate
context: Your corporate smartphone battery is at 4% right before boarding. There is a public USB charging kiosk with open USB-A ports offering 'Free High-Speed Charge'.
dilemma: Should you plug your phone directly into the public USB kiosk port?

choices.text: Plug directly in using a standard data cable because you need battery.
choices.feedback: 'Juice Jacking' risk! Modified charging kiosks can initiate unauthorized data sync or install mobile exploits over USB data lines.

choices.text: Use your own AC wall adapter into an electrical power outlet, or use a data-blocking USB 'condom' that only passes power pins.
choices.feedback: Safe power management! Using AC outlets prevents all data transmission.

choices.text: Plug it into a stranger's laptop at the gate.
choices.feedback: Untrusted endpoint connection risks bidirectional compromise.

title: The Public Figma Architecture Diagram
context: You created a Figma board illustrating the complete database schema, microservice topology, and private IP subnets of the corporate cloud platform. You want to share it with an external freelance designer.
dilemma: How should you configure the Figma sharing link?

choices.text: Set link access to 'Anyone with the link can view' for convenience.
choices.feedback: Major risk! Public links are routinely indexed by search bots or accidentally leaked, revealing internal network architecture.

choices.text: Restrict access to authenticated email addresses only, require password/SSO, and omit internal IP subnets from visual diagrams.
choices.feedback: Strict access governance ensures network blueprints are visible only to verified collaborators.

choices.text: Post the Figma link in a public Reddit design forum to ask for feedback.
choices.feedback: Severe violation of Non-Disclosure and Confidentiality standards.

title: Sharing Admin Account for Production Hotfix
context: A critical production bug occurs on a Saturday night. The lead DevOps engineer is on a flight without Wi-Fi. A teammate asks you: 'Do you have Dave's root database password or can we log into his AWS admin console?'
dilemma: Should you share credentials or use someone else's admin login?

choices.text: Share Dave's password if you know it, because fixing the outage is urgent.
choices.feedback: Violates Sec 2.2 (Account Segregation). Shared logins destroy audit trails and non-repudiation.

choices.text: Follow the designated Emergency Break-Glass procedure where temporary elevated access is provisioned to a unique named identity with full session recording.
choices.feedback: Compliant emergency response. Preserves accountability while enabling swift resolution.

choices.text: Disable the production firewall temporarily so everyone can log in without passwords.
choices.feedback: Catastrophic security failure that invites immediate automated compromise.
